In addition, \na written safe procedure for performing the job must be developed. \n5.18   LOTO for Industrial Vehicles \n5.18.1 Any vehicle has the potential to contain various types of hazardous energy: \n Mechanical hazards associated with start-up. \n Mechanical motions due to moving power transmission components. \n Mechanical hazards with disc brake springs and tire components. \n Hydraulic hazards associated with fluid pressure and loss. \n Gravitational energy from elevated vehicles and lifts. \n Gravitational energy from elevated truck-mounted equipment such as dump beds. \n Airbag explosion. \n Electric battery shock, arc, or burns. \n Fuel and fluid system fire or explosion. \n Hot or cryogenic fluid and surface hazards. \n Chemical energy (e.g., battery acid, coolants, lubricants, etc.). \n5.18.2 Before servicing an industrial vehicle, an initial step is to remove the ignition key from \nthe ignition switch.  \n The repairperson shall maintain sole possession of that key, placing it in their pocket \nor a group lockout box if more than one person is servicing the vehicle. \n Doors to the vehicle should also be locked. \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 38 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 38 of 52 \n5.18.3 If the above two steps are insufficient to prevent an engine from accidentally starting, \nthe repair person shall disconnect the battery cables. \n Disconnecting batteries is essential when working on or around cooling fans, which \ncan automatically start up after removing the ignition key. \n It is good to allow an engine to cool down sufficiently. Doing so will allow heat and \nsubsequent pressure to dissipate, helping control those forms of hazardous energy. \n5.18.4 Depending on the type of vehicle being worked on and the service being performed, \nthe repair person must either lower or block-up components held up by hydraulic \npressure, such as dump beds and aerial lifts. It may also be necessary to chock or \nblock wheels to prevent a vehicle from rolling. \n5.18.5 Dump beds can be incredibly perplexing. Manufacturer-provided props often do not \nprovide the clearance necessary to perform many under-bed repairs. This incites some \nrepair persons to create their support braces, many of which do not provide adequate \nprotection.  \n The equipment manufacturer shall be contacted to discuss an alternative body prop \nor another suitable method to perform the work. \n Remember that reenergizing a vehicle or component is often necessary for testing or \ntroubleshooting.  \n A procedure that defines the sequence of actions necessary to accomplish the task \nsafely shall be developed. \n5.18.6 It is imperative to check its service guidelines with the specific industrial vehicle \nmanufacturer. Those service guidelines can double as guidelines to help develop \nenergy isolation and verification procedures. \n5.18.7 Thorough energy isolation and verification procedures must be developed for shop \nequipment, including lifts, jacks, tire changers, wheel balancers, and pneumatic \n(compressed air) systems.  \n Procedures should be aligned with the equipment manufacturers’ service guidelines. \n \n It is essential that the industrial vehicle energy isolation and training program helps to \nensure that employees understand all relevant energy sources, methods of isolating \nor controlling those energy sources, and methods to verify effective energy control. \nTherefore, employee retraining may be necessary from time to time.  \n \n \n \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 39 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 39 of 52 \n5.19  Tagout Alternative/ Tagout System Limitations \n5.19.1 A tag must only be used instead of an equipment lock when there is no means to apply \na lock. \n5.19.2 If a machine cannot be locked out, it must be tagged. If energy isolating devices \ncannot accommodate locks, a tag shall be used to warn employees that a machine is \nde-energized for servicing. \n5.19.3 The procedure for installing and removing tags is the same as the lockout procedure. \n5.19.4 Tags are only a warning device affixed to energy isolating devices and do not provide \nthe physical restraint on those devices provided by a lock. \n5.19.5 When a tag is attached to an energy isolating means, it is not to be removed without \nauthorization from the authorized person responsible. It is also never to be bypassed, \nignored, or otherwise defeated. \n5.19.6 Tags must be legible and understandable by all authorized employees, affected \nemployees, and all other employees whose work operations are or may be in the area \nto be effective. \n5.19.7 Tags and their means of attachment must be made of materials that will withstand the \nenvironmental conditions encountered in the workplace. \n5.19.8 Employees shall be made to understand that tags may evoke a false sense of security \nand their meaning need to be understood as part of the overall energy control \nprogram. \n5.19.9 Tags must be securely fastened to the energy isolating devices so they cannot be \ninadvertently or accidentally detached during use. \n5.19.10 Tags shall include the employee's name, division, and date. \n5.19.11 Like a lock, the tag must be securely fastened, in a position to be seen by all \nemployees, and standardized. Therefore, the following safety tags (Figure 9) have \nbeen standardized, and no others are permitted to be used: \n \nFigure 9 (Above) - Approved Durable Tag with Grommet \n\n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 40 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 40 of 52 \n5.20 Alternative Control - Requirements \n5.20.1 You cannot use control circuit type devices such as start/stop push buttons, e-stops, \nselector switches, presence sensing devices, or limiting switches instead of energy-\nisolating devices for equipment lockout. This is because these control circuit type \ndevices do not physically isolate equipment from the equipment’s energy source. As a \nresult, unanticipated circumstances such as welded contacts or a loose wire shorting \nout can cause unexpected energization or startup.  \n5.20.2 Under the “minor servicing,” circuitry meeting the control reliability requirements of \nANSI Z244.1-2016 provides the alternative control measures required to control \nhazardous energy. \n Control reliability is the capability of the control system and related interfacing to \nachieve a safe state in the event of a failure. \n \n For example, an interlock or e-stop having a dual-channel (redundant) circuit with \na self-monitoring safety module typically meets the control reliability \nrequirements. \n A basic start/stop circuit is equipped with a single-contact button (single channel), \neven though it may be “safety-rated” (positive contacts). \n Due to the number of times the e-stop is cycled and the simplicity of the circuit, \nthere are still several chances for a single component to fail, leading to circuit \nfailure.  \n Because of the lack of redundancy and self-checking circuitry, this single-channel \ne-stop circuit is not considered control reliable.  \n \n If you are considering incorporating control reliable safety control circuits, a thorough \npracticability/justification analysis (CCS-HSS-FRM-0009.0), risk assessment (CCS-\nHSS-FRM-0010.0), and other alternative control evaluations (see Appendix A) must \nbe done to document and verify the necessary integrity and performance levels of the \ncontrol system. This ensures you are providing equivalent and effective employee \nprotection. \n \n The machine supplier, competent machine integrator, or internal engineering delegate \ncan only make the above control reliable safety control circuits determination. These \npersons can determine a machine’s performance level according to (EN) ISO \nstandards which correspond to the machine performance level expectations. \nMachines with interlocks, e-stops, or presence sensing technologies have an up-to-\ndate (no significant changes made to machine or wiring) machine performance level \nreview on file.  \n5.20.3 The exemption for minor tool changes and adjustments and other minor servicing \nactivities is a unique situation and shall not be used to avoid lockout/tryout. \n5.20.4 Lockout/tryout shall be used unless the division manager can demonstrate to the \nHealth, Safety, and Security Manager that an alternative control provides equal or \ngreater protection. When energy isolation is not used, approved alternative control \nshall be used. \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 41 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 41 of 52 \n5.20.5 There are three specific criteria to determine if the minor servicing exception would \napply to a particular activity: \n The activity must be conducted during normal production operations. \n The activity must be: \n \n Routine: The activity must be a regular course of procedure and follow established \npractices. \n Repetitive: The activity must be regularly repeated as part of the production \nprocess. \n Integral: The activity must be essential to the production process. \n5.20.6 Before alternative controls are used, the following shall be completed and approved \nper ANSI Z244.1-2016, The Control of Hazardous Energy Lockout and Alternative \nControls: \n A practicability/justification analysis per clause 8.2.1 (CCS-HSS-FRM-0009.0). \n A risk assessment as per clause 8.2.2 (CCS-HSS-FRM-0010.0).  \n Other alternative control evaluations as described in clauses 8.2.3 – 8.2.14 (See \nAppendix A). \n5.20.7 Alternative controls shall be added to the safe job procedure (JSHA or JSA) if \napproved. \n5.20.8 There shall be a master list in each division of these approved alternative controls. \n5.20.9 Alternative controls must be under the exclusive control of the employee performing \nthe minor servicing. \n5.20.10 These alternative controls must enable the employee to safely perform the servicing \ntask without being exposed to the energization or activation of the equipment or the \nrelease of stored energy. \n5.20.11 If the minor servicing exception criteria are not met in full, this Standard is applicable, \nand the equipment or machinery must be de-energized. In addition, all potentially \nhazardous energy must be brought to a zero-energy state. \n5.21 Contract Workers (Contractors, Sub-Contractors, Service Providers) \n5.21.1 When contractors work at a Cleveland-Cliffs Steel facility, they must follow their written \nlockout/tryout standard and adhere to the Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Energy Isolation \nStandard.  \n5.21.2 All contract workers must comply with these requirements, beginning with, but not \nlimited to, having a red personal safety lock and lock identification. \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 42 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 42 of 52 \n5.21.3 Contract workers shall identify personal safety locks with employee and contractor \ncompany names. \n Contract workers are permitted to use a durable tag with a grommet attached to the \nshank of their personal safety lock due to outages and utilization of travelers. \n5.21.4 Contract workers are not permitted to operate any energy isolation devices. If components are used \nthat are less than well-tried or less than well-tried designs are implemented, the \narchitecture/structure can significantly improve the system’s reliability. \n6.12.3 Well-Tried Components \n A well-tried component is a component that is either widely used in the past with \nsuccessful results in similar applications or made and verified by the component \nmanufacturer using principles that demonstrate its suitability and reliability for safety-\nrelated applications. \n The components used can be checked and verified on new machinery and \nequipment and existing equipment used in the field. Thus, both users and suppliers \nof machinery can verify the design of existing machinery in the field. \n6.12.4 Well-Tried Designs \n A well-tried design is a system that has been demonstrated, based on an analysis of \noperational experience, for a specific configuration of an element to show that the \nlikelihood of dangerous systematic faults is acceptably low. \n6.12.5 Common Cause Failure (CCF) \n Common cause failures refer to a failure resulting from one or more events, causing \nconcurrent failures of two or more separate elements in a redundant \narchitecture/structure subsystem, leading to a dangerous failure. \n A CCF usually results in two or more failures from a single event or cause. \nTherefore, the design should be assessed to establish the effectiveness of the \nmeasures used to safeguard against CCF. \n6.12.6 Fault Tolerance \n Fault tolerance pertains to the ability of an alternative control to achieve a safe state \nin the event of a fault. Faults can include leaking valves, electrical shorts, contactors \nwelding shut, mechanical fractures/breakage, overheating components, and \nenvironmental exposure. \n Fault tolerance is determined by the circuit’s architecture and is defined as \ncategories and performance levels in ISO 13849-1 or “Control Reliability” as defined \nin ANSI B11.19. \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 47 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 47 of 52 \n6.12.7 Exclusivity or Individual Control \n Examples include, but are not limited to: \n Locks \n Size of working zone \n Proximity to control stations, pendants, or devices \n Locking devices \n Passwords \n Enabling devices \n Hold to run controls \n Trapped key systems \n Presence sensing devices (under some conditions) \n Interlock blocking device \n RFID systems \n Factors that reduce exclusivity shall be considered in alternate risk reduction \nmeasures \n Examples include, but are not limited to: \n Key reproducibility \n Manual manipulation of controls or devices \n Password protection and management \n Visibility of the hazardous area from the reset location (line of sight) \n6.12.8 Tamper Resistance \n Whereas exclusivity pertains to a person’s ability to control the release of energy, \ntamper resistance refers to the ability of a person to tamper intentionally, resulting in \na system inadvertently energizing or releasing energy. A lock exhibits good tamper \nresistance due to the physical properties of the lock. Tagout has less tamper \nresistance as defeating a plastic zip tie requires less force and more easily obtained \ntools (for example, pliers versus bolt cutters). A warning or tag exhibits even less \ntamper resistance. \n Selection of system components may also serve to resist tampering (bypass, \njumpering, defeat of interlocks, etc.). \n The physical layout of the equipment may achieve tamper resistance. For example, \nrestricting access to areas is another form of physical layout that improves tamper \nresistance. \n The physical configuration of components may also achieve tamper resistance. \nDesigns that limit or prohibit mechanical manipulation of the controls improve tamper \nresistance. \n Tamper resistance need not be physical. For example, passwords that restrict \naccess represent another form of tamper resistance. \n Another form of tamper resistance is technical sophistication or complexity. Tamper \nresistance is improved if bypassing a system requires having access to, and being \nable to read, the system schematics. Systems requiring specialized skills to operate \nhave greater tamper resistance than those without. \n \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 48 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 48 of 52 \n6.12.9 Program to Support \n The documentation of the tasks which may be performed using a specific alternative \ncontrol is intended to prevent task creep. \n6.12.10 Procedures in Place \n The procedures in place to support an alternative control shall be evaluated. \nAlternative controls shall include developing, documenting, and using \nprocedures when affected persons are engaged in activities requiring the \ncontrol of hazardous energy. \n6.12.11 Periodic Check and Test \n Where alternative controls are used to control hazardous energy, the need for \nchecking is especially important because, over time, equipment, operations, and \nwork methods can change in small and large ways. Without a program that requires \nperiodic checking and testing, alternative controls can become outdated to the point \nthat they no longer provide adequate protection. \n Checking and testing shall also include correcting any deviations or inadequacies \nidentified. \n6.12.12 Review by a Qualified Person \n The persons developing the alternative control should use due diligence throughout \nthe process to achieve high confidence in the results. Confidence can be improved \nby consulting others with the appropriate knowledge and expertise and having other \nqualified persons review the design. \n \n  \n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 49 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 49 of 52 \n6.13 Appendix B – Lockout/Tryout Implementation Flow Diagram \n \n \n  \n\n\n--- SOURCE PDF PAGE 50 ---\nEnergy Isolation Safety Standard   \n \nFor reference only.   Invalid if printed.  \nPage 50 of 52 \n6.14 Appendix C – Functional Lockout Flowchart \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n  \nYes \nIs system or  \nequipment in \noperation? \nNo \nIsolate all energy sources \nTurn off all operating controls \nIdentify the type(s) and magnitude of energy \nNotify all affected employees \nFollow normal cycle stop \nor shut down process \nEquipment or process needs \nmaintenance or service where a \nlockout is required \nNo Is system \nproperly locked \nout & tried \nout? Page 2 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 1 Purpose/Scope 1.1 Establish minimum standards for all Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Operations to protect employees and contracted workers that are exposed to potential falls greater than 4 feet or working above dangerous equipment. In addition, it establishes the scope, training, and use of fall protection systems by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees in Cleveland-Cliffs Steel facilities. 1.2 This standard shall establish a means to analyze elevated work tasks, determine appropriate controls and protect personnel from fall to below hazards. All people performing work on Cleveland-Cliffs Steel property shall follow and comply with the requirements in this standard, as it has been developed to meet or exceed applicable OSHA regulatory requirements. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 3 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 2 Responsibilities and Authorities 2.1 This Standard was jointly developed with participation from the represented workforce and management. 2.2 Cleveland-Cliffs Employees and Contractor Employees shall: • Notify supervisors or other management personnel when fall exposures exist and are not adequately controlled. • Attend required training. • Properly wear all required fall protection equipment when performing a task or activity in an unprotected area where a fall potential of greater than 4 feet exist. • Inspect fall protection equipment before use to identify any deficiencies. • Maintain and store personal fall protection equipment following this standard. • Make personal fall protection components available for annual inspection. 2.3 Supervisors and Management Personnel shall in addition to the above: • Assess the work area for potential fall hazards, working-at-height scenarios and use the hierarchy of controls to mitigate fall exposures. • Ensure that only trained and authorized personnel are assigned work that requires fall protection equipment. • Ensure employees attend required fall protection training. • Ensure training is documented and records are available. • Ensure that approved fall protection equipment is available in adequate supply. 2.4 Engineering Department shall: • Ensure a documented process is in place for engineering, inspecting, and testing of fall protection systems. • Confirm the qualification and certification of 3rd party inspectors of engineered systems. • Verify and document structural integrity of roofs and other structures for fall-through protection. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 4 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard • Maintain documents pertaining to fall protection system design as required for regularly scheduled system recertification. 2.5 Purchasing shall: • Ensure only approved fall protection equipment is made available that is compliant with regulatory requirements and Cleveland-Cliffs standards. • Ensure contractors that have the potential for working at heights, understand the requirements stipulated in this Standard, and that contractor personnel have the necessary training to use and wear fall protection equipment. 2.6 Site Safety Department shall: • Establish and maintain guidance and documents in compliance with this Standard. • Review and approve the need for new and additional fall protection equipment, including Engineered Systems and components (Gemtor, Railmaster, etc.) before use. • Audit for compliance with this Standard. • Ensure Fall Protection Training is made available and is conducted in compliance with this Standard. • Conduct investigation for all fall to below incidents. • Evaluate employee needs for special harnesses or other alternative fall protection needs. Page 6 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 3.2 Definitions Anchorage or Anchorage Point: A secure point of attachment for lifelines, lanyards, or deceleration devices capable of supporting 5,000 pounds per person or is designed by a qualified person and are a part of a complete fall protection system maintaining a safety factor of at least two. Arresting Force: The force generated by arresting the test weight that is transmitted through the fall arresting system components to the anchorage or load cell. Authorized Person: A person approved or assigned to perform a specific type of duty or duties or to be at a specific location or job site (e.g., building maintenance, roof repair, etc.). Employees who are required to wear fall protection during work activities. Body Harness: A design of straps which may be secured about the employee in a manner that will distribute the fall arrest forces over at least the thighs, pelvis, waist, chest, and shoulders with means for attaching it to other components of a personal fall arrest system. Competent Person: A person who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards in any personal fall protection system or any component of it, as well as in their application and uses with related equipment, and who has authorization to take prompt, corrective action to eliminate the identified hazards. Cage/Basket Guard: An enclosure that is fastened to the side rails of the fixed ladder or to the structure to encircle the climbing space of the ladder for the safety of the person who must climb the ladder. Connector: A device used to couple (connect) parts of the personal fall arrest system together. Carabiner: A connector component comprised of a trapezoidal or oval-shaped body with a normally closed gate. The gate, when released, automatically closes to retain the object. All carabiners used in fall protection systems must be the automatic locking type and have a minimum tensile strength of 5,000 pounds (22 kN). Dangerous Equipment: Equipment (such as pickling or galvanizing tanks, degreasing units, machinery, electrical equipment, and other units) which, as a result of form or function, may be hazardous to employees who fall onto or into such equipment. Deceleration Device: Any mechanism which serves to lessen the arresting force on the body during a fall. Deceleration Distance: The vertical distance a falling employee travels from the point at which the deceleration device begins to operate, excluding lifeline elongation and free fall distance, until stopping. It is measured as the distance between the location of an employee's body harness attachment point at the moment of activation (at the onset of fall arrest forces) of the deceleration device during a fall, and the location of that attachment point after the employee comes to a full stop. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 7 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Fall Arrest System: A system that prevents a worker from falling and contacting a lower level. It consists of an anchorage, connectors, a full body harness, and may include a lanyard, deceleration device, lifeline, or any combination of the before-mentioned items. Fall Clearance Calculation: The total calculated distance required to prevent workers from hitting the ground or lower level, in case of a fall. Free Fall: The act of falling before a personal fall arrest system begins to apply force to arrest the fall. Free Fall Distance: The vertical displacement of the fall arrest attachment point on the employee's body harness between the onset of the fall and just before the system begins to apply force to arrest the fall. This distance excludes deceleration distance, and lifeline/lanyard elongation, but includes any deceleration device slide distance or self-retracting lifeline/lanyard extension before they operate and fall arrest forces occur. (Always minimize Free Fall Distance not to exceed 6 feet.) Fixed Ladder: A ladder which is permanently attached to a structure, building or equipment. (Does not include ship stairs, step bolts or manhole steps.) All new or modified fixed ladders greater than 24 feet shall have a ladder safety system or fall arrest system. Existing fixed ladders must have a ladder safety system or fall arrest system by November 2036. Guardrail System: A barrier erected along an unprotected or exposed side, edge, or other areas of a walking/working surface to prevent workers from falling to a lower level. The system consists of a top rail at 42 inches (plus or minus three inches) above the walking surface, a midrail at a height midway between the top edge of the guardrail and the walking surface. A toe board is required to ensure falling object protection along the exposed edge of overhead walking/working surfaces sufficient to protect employees below. Handrail System: A barrier erected to prevent employees from falling to lower levels. Handrails are not less than 30 inches and not more than 38 inches measured from the edge of the stair tread. There must be a minimum of 2.5 inches clearance between the handrail and any other object. Lanyard: A flexible line of rope, cable, or strap with self-locking snap hook connectors at each end for connecting to body harnesses or deceleration devices. Ladder Safety System: A system (usually consisting of a carrier, safety sleeve, lanyard, connectors, and body harness) attached to a fixed ladder designed to eliminate or reduce the possibility of a worker falling from the ladder. Leading Edge: The edge of a floor, roof or other walking/working surface which changes location as additional floor, roof, etc., is placed or constructed. A leading edge is considered an unprotected side or edge. Lifeline: A component consisting of a flexible line for connection to an anchorage at one end to hang vertically (vertical lifelines), or for connection to anchorages at both ends to stretch horizontally (horizontal lifeline), and which serves as a means for connecting other components of a personal fall arrest system to the anchorage. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 8 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Low-Slope Roof: A roof having a slope less than or equal to 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal). Personal Fall Arrest System: System used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. It consists of an anchorage, connectors, full body harness and a self-retractable lifeline/lanyard. Personal Fall Protection: A system that is used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. The fall protection must consist of a full body harness, a lanyard with a deceleration device and an anchorage or lifeline with approved hooking devices as specified in Cleveland- Cliffs Fall Protection Standard. Qualified Person: One who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge, training and experience, has successfully demonstrated ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work or the project. Rope Grab: A cam-type deceleration device that travels on a lifeline and automatically engages the lifeline and locks to arrest an employee’s fall. Safety Factor: An added margin of security against risk. Safety Net Systems: A horizontal or semi-horizontal, cantilever-style barrier that uses a netting system to stop falling workers before they contact a lower level or obstruction. Safety Monitor: A competent person responsible for recognizing and warning workers of fall hazards. Self-Retracting Lifeline/Lanyard: Deceleration device containing a drum-wound line which can be slowly extracted from, or retracted onto, the drum under slight tension during normal employee movement, and which after the onset of a fall, automatically locks the drum and arrests the fall. Steep Roof: Roof having slope of greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal). Snap Hook: A connector comprised of a hook-shaped member with a closed keeper, which may be opened to permit the hook to receive an object, and when released, automatically closes to retain the object. Snap hooks must be self-closing with a self-locking keeper, which remains closed and locked until unlocked and pressed open for connection or disconnection, thus preventing the opportunity for the object to “roll out” of the snap hook. Snap hooks used for fall protection systems must have a 3,600-pound gate strength. Swing Fall: The potential for a worker using a personal fall arrest system to fall and swing in a pendulum motion, subjecting the worker to strike a fixed object or other hazards. This can occur if a worker falls and the anchorage is not directly overhead, and a fall allows the worker to swing toward the anchor point. Tie Off: The act of a person wearing personal fall protection equipment, connecting directly to an anchorage point. 100 % tie off is required when exposed to a fall hazard while using Travel Restraint or Fall Arrest systems. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 9 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard Toe Board: A solid horizontal guard installed along the exposed edge of overhead walking/working surfaces to prevent the fall of materials and equipment to lower levels and protect employees below. They must be a minimum of 3.5 inches and not have an opening more than 0.25 inches above the walking/working surface. Total Fall Distance: Adding the free fall distance, lanyard deceleration distance depending on the equipment (24” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class A, 54” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class B, 42” for ANSI Z359.14-2021 Class 1 and Class 2), harness stretch, the distance your body extended from the dorsal ring of your harness attached to your anchorage point, and a 3-foot safety factor. Trauma Straps: A pair of straps attached to a full body harness that allows a worker, who is suspended, to stand up in their harness and to relieve the pressure being applied to the arteries and veins around the top of the legs. Travel Restraint (Tether) Line: A rope or wire rope used to transfer forces from a body support to an anchorage or anchorage connector in a travel restraint system. Travel Restraint System: A combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection) and body support intended to be used by an employee to limit travel to prevent exposure to a fall hazard. A travel restraint system is used such that it does not support any portion of the employee's weight; otherwise, the system would be a positioning system or a personal fall arrest system. Travel restraint lines must be capable of sustaining a tensile load of at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN). Unprotected Sides or Edges: Any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface; e.g., floor, roof, ramp, or runway where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches high. Walking/Working Surface: Any surface, whether horizontal or vertical, on which an employee walks or works, including but not limited to floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, framework, and concrete reinforcing steel. Work Positioning: A system consisting of a body harness, lanyards, and anchorage devices rigged to allow a person to be supported on an elevated vertical surface, such as a wall or fixed ladder, and work with both hands free. Attachments should be at the workers hips as preferred method while using a work positioning system. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 11 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5 Requirements 5.1 Application 5.1.1 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees, contractors, sub-contractors, service providers, vendors and visitors when working at any elevation greater than four (4) feet from the floor, deck, platform, or ground level that is not adequately protected on all sides by standard handrails or guardrails shall be required to use personal fall protection. 5.1.2 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees, contractors, sub-contractors, service providers, vendors, and visitors when at any elevation above dangerous equipment shall be protected from falling into or onto the dangerous equipment by guardrails, equipment guards or appropriate fall protection systems. 5.1.3 Cleveland-Cliffs Steel employees, contractors, sub-contractors, service providers, vendors and visitors working in an aerial lift, scissors lift, on scaffolding without standard handrail or exposed to a fall hazard around an excavation (4 feet or deeper) are also required to use personal fall protection. 5.1.4 Every effort must be made by all workers to eliminate falls to a lower level or into or onto dangerous equipment. 5.1.5 Use the Take 5 process to assess the job and use the Hierarchy of Controls when controlling fall to below hazards. Examples: • Eliminate the need for elevated work by moving valves to floor level. • Guard from falls by installing permanent standard railing. • Use scaffolding with handrails, mid-rails, and toe boards. • Use aerial lifts. • Use travel restraint when other exposure-based controls are not available. • Use fall arrest systems when the work doesn’t allow for higher-level controls. • Safety Net System as the last line of protection when no other can be achieved. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 12 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.1.6 Distance alone from a fall to below hazard does not afford adequate protection. 5.1.7 All roofs at Cleveland-Cliffs Steel require fall off and fall through protection. Refer to the plant’s specific roof access procedure. Fall off protection must be used anytime an employee is not protected by standard walkway and handrails or other engineered system. Barricade and restrict access to roofs or other working surfaces where structural integrity concerns exist or where known fall hazards exist. 5.1.8 Travel Restraint devices are used to prevent employees from approaching an area where he or she may fall, such as in aerial and scissors lifts and other personal lifting devices. Only full-body harnesses are permissible as Travel Restraint devices. Lanyards used with the harness must have double locking snap hooks or double locking carabineers. 5.1.9 Travel Restraint systems shall require: • Full body harness equipped with trauma straps. • Non-shock absorbing lanyard. • Lanyard must be of a length that will not allow access to the fall hazard. • Anchorage capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds per user or designed by a qualified person and are a part of a complete fall protection system maintaining a safety factor of at least two. • Any required welding on anchorage must be conducted by a person certified for the specific application and engineering specifications. The person must be certified for the welds required. Contact plant engineering for welding or attachment requirements prior to installation. 5.1.10 Personal fall arrest systems shall require: ABC A. Anchorage Point/Anchorage Connector • Anchorage capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds per user or designed by a qualified person and are a part of a complete fall protection system maintaining a safety factor of at least two. • Any required welding on anchorage must be conducted by a person certified for the specific application and engineering specifications. The person must be certified for the welds required. Contact plant engineering for welding or attachment requirements prior to installation. • Anchorage is to be installed directly overhead when possible. • Workers should not walk more than six (6) feet away from anchorage when possible. B. Full body harness equipped with trauma straps. C. Connecting Device. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. The surfaces shall be smooth and free of sharp edges. Note: Identify and document all electrical fall hazards. If an arc-rated harness is used when working near energized electrical sources, refer to the arc-rated harness manufacturers’ guidelines regarding recommended lanyard and connecting means. 5.1.15 All self-retractable lifeline/lanyard, full body harnesses and associated hardware shall be inspected before and after each use. 5.1.16 The anchorage (tie-off point) shall be capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds per employee attached. If there is any doubt about the strength of the anchorage point, DO NOT TIE OFF; find an alternate anchorage point. 5.1.17 Employee and tools over 310 pounds: Ensure the combined weight (tools and body) does not exceed the limits of the equipment. If the system is used by an employee having a combined weight (tools and body weight) of 310 pounds or more, special personal fall arrest equipment will need to be ordered to accommodate the individual. Please contact the Safety Department for proper equipment, training and job set up if a special harness is needed. ∆ ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Page 14 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.1.18 If any part of a fall protection system is subjected to a free fall, all components shall be taken out of service immediately and given to the Safety Department for discussion with competent persons and disposition. 5.1.19 If any employee experiences a free fall, the Safety Department shall be notified immediately. 5.2 Engineered Systems 5.2.1 Lifeline systems must be engineered to have appropriate anchorages, the strength of line designed to hold a specific number of individuals connected to it, line strength to aid in the arrest of a fall, and durability to hold a fallen employee(s) suspended until a rescue can occur. Only a Qualified Person may design a fall protection system or certify an existing system or anchorage point. 5.2.2 Engineered Systems and components (Gemtor, Railmaster, etc.) must be reviewed by a competent person prior to the Safety Department’s approval to purchase and/or use. A competent person reviews the installation as a part of the fall protection system. 5.3 Tie off Procedures 5.3.1 When using a full-body harness for fall protection, connecting devices shall be attached to the D-ring in the middle of the back, unless the manufacturer provides an approved connector (e.g., Dual Leg Personal SRL). 5.3.2 Snap hooks, including pelican hooks and carabiners, shall be of a design, size, and be compatible with the member that they are attached in order to prevent unintentional disengagement by depression of the keeper or side loading the keeper beyond its rating. 5.3.3 Side D-rings are for travel restraint or work positioning only and shall never be used for fall arrest connections. Whenever possible, tie off to an anchorage point at or above the D-ring of the harness. 5.3.4 For fall arrest systems on ladder safety systems, a front D-ring will be used or a back D- ring will be used based on the system design. 5.3.5 All new or modified fixed ladders that extend more than 24 feet shall have a ladder safety system or fall arrest system. Existing fixed ladders must have ladder safety system or fall arrest system by November 2036. 5.3.6 Workers shall tie off in a manner that ensures no lower level is struck during a free fall. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 15 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.3.7 Completely understand Fall Clearance Distance. This is the total distance for the fall arrest equipment to stop a fall plus a 3-foot safety factor. Always consider the following when determining fall protection equipment and proper tie-off location: • Location and height of the anchorage. • Free Fall Distance. • The maximum arrest or deceleration distance, depending on the equipment (24” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class A, 54” for ANSI Z359.14-2014 Class B, 42” for ANSI Z359.14-2021 Class 1 and Class 2). Class 1 must be attached to an anchor at or above the D-ring. • The distance that any deployable device will expand. • Stretch of harness and other components. • The height of the employee. • Swing Fall or deflection of non-rigid anchors such as horizontal lifelines. • Safety factor of 3 feet. • Workers should not walk more than six (6) feet away from anchorage, when possible, to minimize free fall distance and swing fall. • Add length of D-ring Extension if applicable. ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Wear the lanyard in such a manner that it will not get caught on or in equipment, structures or moving machinery. No part of the lanyard shall be allowed to dangle freely when not tied off. Page 18 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.3.15 Transitioning from Aerial Lift/Platform • If transition from the aerial platform to another location must be made, a hazard assessment shall be completed to ensure that the fall hazard has either been eliminated, or 100% fall protection tie off (twin leg lanyard) is used. • When transitioning, one leg of the employee’s twin-leg (or Y) lanyard must be attached to an approved connection point in the work area being entered. The other leg of the lanyard must be tied off to the anchorage point of the aerial lift. • The same procedure must be followed when re-entering the aerial lift from the work location. • Workers in an aerial lift or scissors lift will not wear fall arrest systems unless the lift and the attachment points have been specifically designed to meet all requirements of a fall arrest anchoring system and the requirements of this document. The fall protection system must be designed to comply with the anchorage provided by the manufacturer and appropriate use. 5.4 Crane Runway Fall Protection 5.4.1 The fall arrest anchor system must be designed by a qualified person from either the Engineering Department or outside engineering firm. 5.4.2 Whenever possible, the cable height must be set high enough above crane runway girder to ensure clearances and limit fall arrest distance. In addition, where possible, the cable is to be over entire length of both sides of all crane runways. 5.4.3 When using horizontal lifelines for fall protection on crane runways, the employee shall make sure the lifeline is certified and inspected. All horizontal lifelines must be recertified every five years and illegible tags must be replaced at that time. Dual-leg lanyards are necessary to meet OSHA standards when the person comes to a column and must hook the second leg to the cable on the opposite side of the column before unhooking the first leg. 5.5 Handrail and Guardrail Systems 5.5.1 Handrails and guardrails must be made from steel unless the environment dictates the material requires protection from corrosion. Existing wood, chain and wire rope protection shall be replaced. Wood, chain, and wire rope may be used for barriers only. The minimum clearance between the handrail and any other object is 2.5 inches. Where physically possible, access gates used for fall protection should be swing gates designed to not open in the direction of the fall exposure. 5.5.2 Guardrail systems must have a rail at 42 inches (plus or minus 3 inches) above the walking surface, a midrail at a height midway between the top edge of the guardrail and the walking surface, installed so that openings do not exceed 19 inches at its least dimension. A minimum 3.5-inch toe board must be installed along the exposed edge of overhead walking-working surfaces to protect employees below. For stair rail systems, built before January 17, 2017, the top rail may serve as a handrail, provided the top rail is 36 to 38 inches in height. For stair rail systems installed on or after January 17, 2017, the top rail and handrail must be separate. The top rail must be at least 42 inches in height and the handrail must be 30 to 38 inches in height. Guardrails and handrails must withstand 200 pounds of force in any direction. 5.5.3 These handrails and guardrails will be placed in the following areas if necessary or feasible based on job location or requirements: ∆ Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 20 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard • On all open sided floors. • Elevated platforms, walkways, and other elevated walking/working surfaces. • Tops of vessels, tanks and other structures or equipment that could be accessed by personnel. • Around all open excavations or pits over 4 feet deep. • On edges of roofs to provide fall off protection when the roof is structurally sound. 5.6 Inspection 5.6.1 Each plant will establish a process for full body harnesses, lanyards, and their accessories to be inventoried. 5.6.2 Personal fall arrest systems shall be inspected prior to each use for wear, damage, and other deterioration. Defective components shall be removed from service and destroyed. The employee shall inspect all fall protection equipment for damage or excessive wear. 5.6.3 Full Body Harness Inspection 5.6.3.1 Harness straps are to be inspected by beginning at one end, holding the body side of the harness towards you, grasp the harness with your hands 6 to 8 inches apart. Bend the harness strap in an inverted \"U\". The surface tension resulting makes damaged fibers or cuts easier to see. Follow this process the entire length of the harness. Watch for frayed edges, broken fibers, pulled stitches, cuts or chemical/burn damage. 5.6.3.2 Check the D-ring and D-ring metal wear pad (if any) for distortion, cracks, breaks and rough or sharp edges. 5.6.3.3 Attachment of buckles and D-rings should be given special attention. Note any unusual wear, frayed, cut fibers or distortion of the buckles or D-rings. Rivets must be tight and unmovable with fingers. The body side rivet base and outer rivet burr must be flat against the material. Bent rivets will fail under stress. 5.6.3.4 Inspect for frayed or broken strands. Broken webbing strands generally appear as tufts on the webbing surface. Any broken, cut or burned stitches will be readily seen. 5.6.3.5 The tongue or billets of the leg straps receive heavy wear from repeated buckling and unbuckling. Inspect for loose, distorted, or broken grommets. Straps must never have additional punched holes. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 21 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.6.3.6 Buckle tongues must be free of distortion in shape and motion. They must overlap buckle frames and move freely back and forth in their socket. The roller must turn freely on the frame. Check for distortion or sharp edges. 5.6.3.7 Trauma straps must be present and not damaged. 5.6.3.8 Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer as provided in training. 5.6.4 Lanyard Inspection. 5.6.4.1 Travel Restraint Lanyard Inspection: When inspecting lanyards, begin at one end and work to the opposite end. Slowly rotate the lanyard so that the entire circumference is checked. Stitched (spliced) ends require extra attention. 5.6.4.2 The double locking snaps will be inspected closely for hook and eye distortions, cracks, corrosion, or pitted surfaces. The keeper (latch) must seat into the nose without binding and not be distorted or obstructed. The keeper spring will exert sufficient force to firmly close the keeper. Keeper locks must prevent the keeper from opening when the keeper closes. 5.6.4.3 The thimble must be firmly seated in the eye of the splice, and the splice must have no loose or cut strands. In addition, the edges of the thimble must be free of sharp edges, distortions, or cracks. 5.6.4.4 While bending a web lanyard over a pipe or mandrel, observe each side of the webbing. This will reveal any cuts or breaks, swelling, discoloration, cracks, charring or obvious signs of chemical or heat damage. 5.6.4.5 Rotation of the rope lanyard while inspecting from end to end will reveal any fuzzy, worn, broken, or cut fibers. Weakened areas from extreme loads will appear as a noticeable change in original diameter. The rope diameter must be uniform throughout, following a short break-in period. 5.6.4.6 Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer as provided in training. 5.6.5 Snap hooks (including carabineers). 5.6.5.1 Snap hooks must be of the locking type designed and used to prevent disengagement of the snap hook by the contact of the snap hook keeper by the connected member. Snap hooks must be proof tested by the manufacturer to a minimum tensile load of 3,600 pounds, (normal 5,000 pounds) without cracking, breaking, or taking permanent deformation. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 22 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.6.5.2 The keeper of the snap hook must have a spring tension that will not allow the keeper to open with a weight of 25 pounds or less, but the keeper must begin to open with a weight of 4 pounds supported on the keeper against the end of the nose. 5.6.5.3 Inspection of the snap hook must include: • Signs of cracking. • Sharp edges. • Signs of breaking. • Permanent deformation. • Pitted or corroded surfaces. • Keeper must seat properly without binding or obstruction. • Keeper spring must exert sufficient force to ensure closure. • Locks must prevent keeper from opening. 5.6.6 Inspection of Retractable Lanyards: • Anchorage connectors shall be checked for bent, cracked, or distorted components. • With the device in the mounted position, test the lanyard retraction and tension by pulling out several feet of the lanyard and allowing it to retract back into the unit. Always maintain a light tension on the lanyard as it retracts. The lanyard should pull out freely and retract all the way back into the unit. a. If the lanyard does not pull out smoothly or sticks when retracting, pull the entire lanyard out of the housing and allow it to retract slowly under tension. b. The lanyard must be checked for signs of damage. Inspect for cuts, burns, corrosion, kinks, frays or worn areas. Inspect any sewing for loose, broken, or damaged stitches. • The braking mechanism shall be tested by grasping the lifeline above the impact indicator (if equipped) and applying a sharp, steady pull downward which will engage the brakes. There should be no slippage of the lifeline while the brakes are engaged. Once tension is released, the brakes will disengage, and the unit will return to the retractable mode. • Check the snap hook to ensure that it operates freely and locks. Inspect the snap hook for any signs of damage to the keepers and any bent, cracked, or distorted components. • Load indicators, if equipped, will typically be located above the snap hook. An indicator will be exposed when subjected to fall arresting forces. Check manufacturer instructions for indicator type and location. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 23 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard • Any additional inspection procedures required by the equipment manufacturer shall be observed. 5.6.7 Visual Indications of Damage to Webbing and Lanyards: 5.6.7.1 Nylon & Cordura: • Heat Damage – In excessive heat, nylon becomes brittle and has a shriveled brownish appearance. In addition, fibers will break when flexed. Therefore, nylon must never be used above 200 degrees Fahrenheit. Refer to limitations listed in the manufacturer’s user manual. • Chemical Damage – Color change usually appears as a brownish smear or smudge. Transverse cracks when harness or lanyard is bent over a pipe. There will also be a loss of elasticity in the harness or lanyard. • Flame/Molten Metal Damage – Webbing strands fuse together. Hard, shiny spots and brittle feel but will not support combustion. • Paint/Solvent Damage – Paint, which penetrates and dries, restricts the movement of fibers. Drying agents and solvents in some paints will appear as chemical damage. 5.6.7.2 Polyester & Dacron: • Heat Damage – Same as nylon above, except do not use above 180 degrees Fahrenheit. Refer to limitations listed in the manufacturer’s user manual. • Chemical Damage – Same as nylon above. • Flame/Molten Metal Damage – Same as nylon above, except will support combustion. • Paint/Solvent Damage – Same as nylon above. 5.6.7.3 Cable: • Slightly bend and rotate the cable. • Visually check for damaged, kinked, broken strands or unusual discoloration or wear patterns. 5.7 Cleaning and Storage of Fall Protection Equipment 5.7.1 Cleaning: Wipe off all surface dirt with a sponge dampened in plain water. Squeeze the sponge dry. Dip the sponge in a mild solution of water and commercial soap or detergent. Work up a thick lather with vigorous back and forth motions. Wipe the belt dry with a clean cloth. Equipment shall hang freely to dry thoroughly without close exposure to heat, steam, or prolonged periods of sunlight. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 24 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.7.2 Never use chemical cleaners such as naphtha, turpentine, acetone, or other similar products. Never use bleach, rubbing alcohol, hydrogen peroxide or other products with sanitizing or disinfecting claims. The effect of these substances on equipment has not been evaluated and may compromise material integrity. 5.7.3 Storage: Never store personal fall arrest equipment on the ground or outdoors exposed to the elements (e.g., sun, rain, snow), or in an area with exposure to harmful substances or corrosive elements. 5.7.4 Refer to the manufacturer’s recommendations for additional cleaning and storage considerations. 5.8 Training 5.8.1 Each employee authorized to wear fall protection equipment shall be trained to recognize the hazards of falling, and procedures to be followed to minimize these hazards. The employee shall be trained by a person who is competent in the following areas: • Nature of fall hazards in the work area and how to recognize them. • The correct procedures for installing, inspecting, operating, maintaining, and disassembling the personal fall protection systems. • The correct use of personal fall protection systems and equipment including, but not limited to, proper hook-up, anchoring and tie-off techniques, and methods of equipment inspection and storage, as specified by the manufacturer. • The use and operation of guardrail systems, personal fall arrest systems and other protection to be used. • Limitations of fall protection system including proper hook-up, anchoring and tie-off techniques. • Requirements set forth in this program and the procedures to be followed to minimize fall hazards. • Emergency and Rescue procedures. 5.8.2 Content of Fall Protection Training • OSHA’s requirements for fall protection. • Contents of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Fall Protection Standard. • Basic skills in fall hazard recognition and control. • Donning and Doffing. • Proper methods of inspecting personal fall protection equipment. • Fall Clearance Calculation methods. • Fall protection systems used at Cleveland-Cliffs Steel. • Hazards associated with fall protection. • Rescue and retrieval requirements. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 25 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.8.3 Training must occur initially before exposure, annually, and when there are changes in the types of fall protection systems or equipment or there are changes in the workplace that render previous training obsolete. 5.8.4 The employee shall be retrained when there is reason to believe the employee does not have the understanding and skill required to follow this procedure. A competent person must conduct any required retraining. 5.8.5 The training shall be documented with the name of the employee, identification number, the date(s) of training and the signature of the person conducting the training. 5.8.6 After the completing the training, a documented quiz or test must be administered to ensure that the employee has acquired the understanding, knowledge and skills necessary to safely perform their duties. 5.9 Safety Net Systems 5.9.1 Safety Net Systems can be used when no other fall protection system is available. Safety Nets must be designed and tested by a qualified person and inspected by a competent person. 5.9.2 A safety net system can be erected in a vertical or horizontal plane or both. It must protect the worker from free falling to a lower level or structure. In addition, it must protect employees from falling tools or debris from the worksite. 5.9.3 Safety nets must be installed as close to the area as possible and must never be more than 30 feet below the highest working surface from which a person may fall. 5.9.4 Nets must be hung with sufficient clearance under them to prevent contact with the surface or structures below when subjected to an impact force equal to the drop test specified by OSHA. 5.9.5 Safety nets and safety net installations must be drop tested at the job site after initial installation before using as a fall protection system, whenever relocated, after major repair, and at six-month intervals, if left in one place. 5.9.6 If it can be demonstrated that it is unreasonable to perform the drop test, a competent person must certify the net and that the net installation is in compliance. 5.9.7 The mesh size of nets must not exceed 6 inches by 6 inches. All new nets must meet accepted performance standards of minimum impact resistance as determined and certified by the manufacturer and must bear a label of proof testing. Border ropes must provide a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 pounds. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 26 of 29 Fall Prevention & Protection Standard 5.9.8 Safety nets must not extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface as described by the OSHA table. Forged steel safety hooks or shackles must be used to fasten the net to its supports. Connections between net panels must develop the full strength of the net. 5.9.9 Net systems must be checked and documented daily and cleaned whenever debris is in the net. Remove any damaged nets for repair or replacement. When nets are removed, no work must take place in that area unless another fall protection system is used. Spare nets may be installed to replace damaged nets if all other components pass an inspection, and a competent person checks the new net. 5.10 Rescue 5.10.1 Emergency and rescue procedures must be developed for rescuing a worker within 10 minutes who has fallen from elevated heights. 5.10.2 An Emergency and Rescue Plan must be developed by the operating department in coordination with the Recue Team. It must include an effective rescue summoning method. It must be in place and discussed prior to any Personal Fall Protection System use. 5.10.3 Emergency teams must be trained on the procedure. 5.11 Investigation of a Fall 5.11.1 All employees involved in a fall arrest or fall must be sent immediately for a medical evaluation to determine the extent of injuries. 5.11.2 All falls must be investigated following Cleveland-Cliffs Steel incident investigation procedures. A competent person in fall protection must attend the investigation as a resource. 5.11.3 Once exposed to a fall, remove fall protection equipment from service immediately and destroy when required after analysis and review by representatives from the Safety and Engineering Departments. Remove the destroyed equipment from any inventory list. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 2 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 1 Purpose/Scope This policy establishes minimum standards for activities that support the inspection, operation, maintenance, boarding/de- boarding, and other safe work practices related to crane operations. This policy applies to employees of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel business units, contractors, subcontractors and hired labor employees performing work for or on behalf of Cleveland-Cliffs Steel on premises owned, rented, or otherwise occupied by Cleveland-Cliffs Steel. The policy applies to Electric Overhead Traveling (EOT) gantry, and semi-gantry cranes including cab, pendent and radio control operated cranes. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 3 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard 2 Responsibilities and Authorities This standard was jointly developed with participation from the represented workforce and management. Qualified Crane Operators Are Responsible For: • Attending crane operator training and following the requirements specified in this standard. • Performing pre-use inspections to ensure cranes are operating properly and to verify that cranes can be operated safely. • Immediately reporting any critical defects or other operational conditions that may affect the safe operation of the crane. • Obeying verbal instructions or hand signals provided by designated shop floor personnel to ensure lifts and crane movements are conducted in a safe manner that avoids potential impact to equipment, personnel, or other objects. • Safely operating cranes and avoiding movements or unsafe practices that can jeopardize the safety of personnel or risk equipment or property damage. • Keeping crane cabs free of clutter and performing necessary housekeeping. • Avoiding distractions or performing other tasks that may take the operators attention away from critical actions required to safely operate the crane. • Using horns or other audible devices to alert ground personnel of the movement of the crane. • Immediately reporting any crane related incidents including personal injuries, near misses or equipment damage events. Printed Copy is for reference only. Refer to the CCS Safety SharePoint site for the most current version. Page 4 of 29 Overhead Crane Safety Standard Qualified Ground Personnel Are Responsible For: • Maintaining awareness of crane operations in their work area and verify safe approach when entering buildings, crossing medians, exiting pulpits or working around crane lifts or other areas where crane operations are conducted. • Receiving approval from the Qualified Crane Operator and verifying conditions to ensure the safe boarding of an occupied crane. • Ensuring appropriate and recognized hand signals or approved radio communications are used to ensure coordination with Qualified Crane Operators. • Suspending crane operations when an unsafe or at-risk condition is observed. • Using sound rigging practices and when necessary, performing low/limited lifts to ensure load stability or to verify the center of gravity of a load. • Using no-touch tools when engaging/disengaging safety latches or when manipulated rigging hardware or lifting cables that are under tension. • Using tag lines or other approved no-touch tools to provide a safe distance when stabilizing, moving, or adjusting suspended loads. • Clearing non-essential personnel from an area where a lift is to be performed and keeping hands and other body parts away from potential pinch points or other hazards associated with crane movements and lifts. 3 References and Definitions References • MIOSHA General Industry R 408.12004 • OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179, Overhead and Gantry Cranes • 29 CFR 1910.181, Derricks • American Society of Mechanical Engineers.
